extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of drama/poetics (playwrights, literature students, dramatic critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing dramatic plots and tragic characters according to Aristotelian principles (unity of action, plot causality, time/place considerations, and the characteristics of the tragic hero). Useful for playwrights, critics, and students of poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dénouement must arise from the plot itself (no Deus ex Machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The λύσις, the unravelling or Dénouement_of the plot, must ... arise out of the plot itself, not by recourse to the Deus ex Machina or to the play of accident.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resolutions that depend on miraculous coincidences, external contrivances, or arbitrary fifth-act devices. The dénouement should be the ‘inevitable, though unexpected, consequences of all that has preceded.’ (Lessing anecdote warns against letting the fifth act 'kill' a play.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole: beginning, middle, and end (their definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end.’ A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity; an end is that which naturally follows some other thing but has nothing following it; a middle follows something and is followed by something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a definite start and finish for the dramatic action. The beginning need not be an absolute origin but should not require tracing causes ad infinitum; the middle must be causally linked to what precedes and follows; the end should conclude the causal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict internal causal sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Within the dramatic action, a strict sequence of cause and effect is prescribed; but the causal chain must not be indefinitely extended outwards.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each incident follows naturally (causally) from previous ones; do not rely on a series of scenes that are only temporally contiguous without inward causal connexion. Avoid plots that invite endless retrograde explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (ἐπεισοδιώδης) plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The opposite holds good of τὸ ἄπειρον ... A succession of stirring scenes does not make a tragedy; and it is just this truth that Euripides is apt to forget when ... he substitutes pathetic effects, striking situations, rapid contrasts and surprises.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble striking or moving scenes merely for effect; ensure scenes are organically connected to the central action and purpose of the play rather than being episodic vignettes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic unity of the drama (vital union of parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The recurring phrase of the Poetics, σύστασις (or σύνθεσις) τῶν πραγμάτων, does not denote a mechanical piecing together of incidents, but a vital union of the parts.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for parts that interweave thought, emotion, will, and external events so they form an organic whole subordinated to a single purpose or end; avoid mechanical or haphazard joining of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action is the controlling law
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The only dramatic Unity enjoined by Aristotle is Unity of Action.’ Unity of Action is the higher and controlling law of the drama; the unities of time and place are secondary and derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize a single, coherent dramatic action and purpose. Time and place constraints should serve that unity, not override it; if a choice must be made, preserve inner logic and unity of action over rigid adherence to time/place rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (guideline, not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun, or but slightly to exceed this limit; whereas the epic action has no limits of time.’ This is recorded as a prevailing practice rather than a strict rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer relatively limited imaginary time for dramatic action (approximately a day), but allow exceptions when dramatic necessity requires longer spans; choral odes and poetic imagination can justify departures from strict temporal equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Place (stage practice; derivative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Place was a stage-practice generally observed in Greek drama but not enjoined explicitly in the Poetics; critics later deduced it from Unity of Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping action within a single locality can help preserve unity, but do not force characters into unnatural behaviour merely to avoid a scene-change. Use general place-names and unchanged stage decoration to aid audience imagination when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as a unifying and time-suspending device
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Chorus formed an ideal bond of union between the separate parts of the action. ... The choral lyrics suspend the outward action of the play, and carry us still farther away from the world of reality.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral odes (or analogous devices) to bridge intervals, idealise elapsed time, and bind dispersed episodes; they can legitimately cover events that are not shown and relax strict chronological demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-specific constraints: drama vs epic
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The action, then, of the drama is concentrated, while that of the epic is large and manifold. ... The epic can admit many episodes ... The drama rejects this multiplicity of incidents; it is of closer tissue, pressing forward to an end which controls its entire structure.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form according to desired breadth: if you want many episodes and extended temporal scope, use epic/novelistic form; if you want concentrated action and immediate representation, use drama and accept its tighter constraints on simultaneity, time, and incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not subordinate inner logic of character to strict unities
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The external rule [of the unities] was thus observed, but at the cost of that inward logic of character and events which is prescribed by the Poetics.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrivances that force characters into implausible choices or compress psychological development solely to satisfy rules about time/place. Preserve believable character motivation and development even if it requires flexible treatment of minor unities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation of place and time is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘After all, the drama is not possible without a certain idealisation of place and time. ... It is part of the poet’s art to make us forget all time; and, if in his company we lose count of months and years, we do not cry out against the impossibility.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ imaginative compression, ellipsis, and poetic devices to make the audience accept temporal and spatial liberties. The goal is dramatic truth and effect, not clock-accurate realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero must produce katharsis of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The function of tragedy is to produce the katharsis of pity and fear; pity being felt for a person who, if not wholly innocent, meets with suffering beyond his deserts; fear being awakened when the sufferer is a man of like nature with ourselves.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design protagonist and catastrophe to elicit both pity and fear. The character should be recognisably human (leading to fear) and undergo undeserved suffering (leading to pity); the plot must support this emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude certain character types from tragic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In the first place, the spectacle of a man eminently good undergoing the change from prosperous to adverse fortune awakens neither pity nor fear. ... Next, and utterly devoid of tragic quality, is the representation of the bad man who experiences the contrary change from distress to prosperity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the tragic protagonist either impeccably virtuous (elicits shock or repulsion rather than pity/fear) or outright villainous (whose downfall/promotion does not produce katharsis). Prefer a character whose moral standing is mixed or middle, so suffering feels tragic rather than merely unjust or merely deserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and catastrophe must be appropriate to evoke tragic emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tragic character must be exhibited through the medium of a plot which has the capacity of giving full satisfaction to these emotions. Certain types, therefore, of character and certain forms of catastrophe are at once excluded, as failing either in whole or in part to produce the tragic effect.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the form of catastrophe and the sequence of events are suited to awaken pity and fear; choose incidents and reversals that reveal character and lead inevitably (by causal sequence) to the tragic outcome rather than relying on arbitrary spectacle.
